meta.label: Cleaning products
meta.attribution: Curated from public ingredient disclosures, certifications (B Corp, EWG, MADE SAFE, Leaping Bunny/Cruelty Free International), brand sustainability pages, and packaging claims - not lab-measured data. Verify current formulas yourself. Reviewed 2026-06. Suggest changes via Contribute.

products.name: Blueland
products.description: A refill-tablet cleaner brand built around reusable bottles, compact shipping and strong low-waste packaging signals.

environment.note: Blueland reports measured impact from its refill model, including plastic diversion, packaging saved and CO2 savings.

transparency.note: Blueland says each product page lists ingredients and associated certifications.

packaging.note: Leaping Bunny describes Blueland tablets in compostable paper for reusable bottles.

cruelty_free.note: Leaping Bunny identifies Blueland as certified cruelty-free.

accessibility.note: Online-first refill system with higher starter-kit cost but lower refill cost than many premium liquids.

products.name: Meliora Cleaning Products
products.description: A Chicago-made cleaner line centered on simple powders, bars, refills, and third-party safer-ingredient certification.

environment.note: MADE SAFE lists Meliora products as certified and notes B Corp, organic raw-product sourcing and 1% for the Planet/WVE partnerships.

transparency.note: Meliora says it lists every ingredient on the label and ingredients page.

packaging.note: Meliora states its line is single-use-plastic-free, with refill/powder/bar formats.

cruelty_free.note: Leaping Bunny lists Meliora Cleaning Products as certified cruelty-free.

accessibility.note: US online and zero-waste retail availability; higher than mainstream pricing but broad enough for online buyers.

products.name: Dr. Bronner's
products.description: A multi-use soap and cleaner brand with unusually deep certification, sourcing and impact-reporting signals.

environment.note: Product certifications include organic and Fair for Life fair-trade supply chains; multi-use soaps reduce product duplication.

transparency.note: Annual All-One reports publish sustainability, sourcing and impact data.

packaging.note: Dr. Bronner's says its refill cartons use 86% less plastic than its 32 oz recycled bottles, with FSC paperboard and a minimal plastic/aluminum lining.

cruelty_free.note: Leaping Bunny lists Dr. Bronner's as certified cruelty-free.

accessibility.note: Widely sold multi-use soap, but more expensive per bottle than basic conventional cleaners.

products.name: AspenClean
products.description: A natural cleaning brand with EWG Verified, Ecocert, vegan, and Leaping Bunny credentials.

environment.note: AspenClean describes EcoCert, EWG and natural cleaning credentials for its product line.

transparency.note: EWG brand pages and EWG Verified status provide ingredient-standard visibility.

packaging.note: Packaging remains mostly conventional recyclable/refill formats rather than plastic-free tablets.

cruelty_free.note: Leaping Bunny lists AspenClean as cruelty-free, vegan-friendly and Ecocert certified.

accessibility.note: Premium North American retail/online availability gives moderate access but higher prices.

products.name: Bio-D
products.description: A UK cleaning brand focused on lower-impact formulas, recycled packaging and vegan/cruelty-free positioning.

environment.note: Bio-D says products use naturally derived ingredients, solar energy, and low-impact manufacturing claims.

transparency.note: Bio-D publishes product/ingredient and accreditation information through its site.

packaging.note: Bio-D says it uses 100% recycled plastic bottles across the range and closed-loop 20L containers.

cruelty_free.note: Bio-D says all products are vegan and cruelty-free, with Vegan Society and Cruelty Free International alignment.

accessibility.note: UK/EU-focused brand with refill/stockist access and mid-market pricing.

products.name: Attitude
products.description: A North American home and personal-care brand with EWG Verified signals and broad retail/online availability.

environment.note: ATTITUDE describes EWG Verified, naturally derived home and personal-care products.

transparency.note: EWG and ATTITUDE pages expose ingredient-standard claims and verification status.

packaging.note: Some refill formats exist, but most products remain in conventional retail packaging.

cruelty_free.note: ATTITUDE positions its line as vegan/cruelty-free alongside EWG verification.

accessibility.note: Online and retail availability across North America/EU, but premium pricing limits access.

products.name: Smol
products.description: A UK/EU refill-by-mail cleaning model with compact packaging and certified vegan/cruelty-free claims.

environment.note: Ethical Consumer notes Smol prohibits many toxic products and uses mostly reusable or plastic-free packaging.

transparency.note: Smol publishes ingredient/help information, though disclosure is less detailed than certification-heavy leaders.

packaging.note: Ethical Consumer reports Smol mostly uses reusable, returnable or plastic-free packaging.

cruelty_free.note: Smol says products are vegan and Leaping Bunny certified via Cruelty Free International.

accessibility.note: Subscription/online UK/EU model is convenient for some but less accessible than supermarkets.

products.name: Branch Basics
products.description: A premium concentrate system meant to replace several household cleaners through refillable bottles.

environment.note: MADE SAFE certified the Branch Basics concentrate as screened for ingredients known or suspected to harm people, animals or environment.

transparency.note: Concentrate model and product pages disclose the formula basis, though less third-party detail than EWG brands.

packaging.note: One concentrate replaces multiple cleaners and supports refillable bottles, cutting duplicate packaging.

cruelty_free.note: Leaping Bunny lists Branch Basics as certified cruelty-free.

accessibility.note: Premium online concentrate has higher upfront cost and lower mainstream retail access.

products.name: Ecover
products.description: A widely available plant-based cleaner pioneer with recycled-plastic and refill work, now under SC Johnson ownership.

environment.note: Ecover describes biodegradable, plant-based products and refill/recycled-plastic work.

transparency.note: Ecover publishes product ingredient information, though ownership by SC Johnson moderates the transparency score.

packaging.note: Ecover states bottles use 100% recycled plastic and promotes refill options.

cruelty_free.note: Vegan cleaning-product guides and Ecover materials identify the line as vegan/cruelty-free, but certification visibility is less clean than Leaping Bunny pages.

accessibility.note: Widely available in UK/EU retail at mid-market prices.

products.name: Seventh Generation
products.description: A mainstream US safer-cleaning brand with strong availability, public ingredient information and Leaping Bunny certification.

environment.note: Seventh Generation reports plant-based/home cleaning products and safer-choice style product lines, though some petrochemical inputs remain.

transparency.note: Seventh Generation publishes product and ingredient information; Commons still notes impact limitations.

packaging.note: Commons notes lower-waste refill options and concentrated formulas for some products, with recycled-plastic packaging common.

cruelty_free.note: Leaping Bunny lists Seventh Generation as certified cruelty-free.

accessibility.note: Mainstream US grocery/online availability makes access strong.

products.name: Common Good
products.description: A refill-centered cleaning brand designed around reusable bottles and plant-based formulas.

environment.note: Common Good describes plant-based soaps, detergents and cleaners with safe/gentle ingredients.

transparency.note: Common Good surfaces ingredient and formulation claims, but with less third-party certification than top-scoring brands.

packaging.note: Common Good centers refillable cleaning products and sustainable packaging.

cruelty_free.note: Common Good describes its line as vegan and cruelty-free.

accessibility.note: Online and refill-partner model is less accessible than national grocery brands.

products.name: Cleancult
products.description: A refillable cleaning system built around reusable bottles and paper-based refill cartons.

environment.note: Cleancult markets recyclable paper-based refills and reusable bottles to reduce plastic waste.

transparency.note: Product pages list ingredient claims but lack the same third-party safer-ingredient certification depth as EWG/MADE SAFE leaders.

packaging.note: Cleancult describes paper-based recyclable refills and reusable forever bottles.

cruelty_free.note: Leaping Bunny describes Clean Cult cleaning products as certified cruelty-free.

accessibility.note: Online plus major US retail availability, including Target/Walmart, makes access stronger than many refill brands.

products.name: Grove Co. cleaning concentrates
products.description: A B Corp/public-benefit marketplace with its own concentrated cleaning refills and broader eco-home assortment.

environment.note: B Lab describes Grove as a B Corp/public-benefit company with carbon-neutral orders and plastic-waste initiatives.

transparency.note: B Corp and public-benefit reporting add company-level accountability, but marketplace product formulas vary.

packaging.note: Grove Co concentrates reduce plastic, while broader marketplace packaging remains mixed.

cruelty_free.note: Many Grove Co items claim cruelty-free, but certification is not as uniform as Leaping Bunny-only brands.

accessibility.note: Broad online subscription marketplace with moderate prices and frequent promotions.

products.name: Method
products.description: A mainstream plant-based cleaning brand with strong retail access and cruelty-free signals, but conventional bottle formats.

environment.note: Method describes planet-friendly cleaning products and a business mission to make cleaning greener.

transparency.note: Method provides transparency/disclosure pages and product information, but less third-party verification than top leaders.

packaging.note: Method is widely associated with recycled-plastic bottles, but remains mostly liquid products in plastic packaging.

cruelty_free.note: Leaping Bunny and brand materials identify Method as cruelty-free, though it is owned by SC Johnson.

accessibility.note: Widely available at mainstream US retailers at mid-market prices.

products.name: Mrs. Meyer's
products.description: A widely available scented cleaner line with some safer-ingredient signals and mainstream affordability.

environment.note: Mrs. Meyer's sustainability page says down-the-drain products meet OECD biodegradability standards and have no added PFAS.

transparency.note: Mrs. Meyer's about page lists ingredients it avoids and explains raw-material choices.

packaging.note: Conventional recyclable bottles keep packaging score moderate rather than refill/plastic-free.

cruelty_free.note: Leaping Bunny lists Mrs. Meyer's Clean Day as cruelty-free.

accessibility.note: Very broad US grocery and mass-retail availability at affordable prices.

products.name: Astonish
products.description: A budget UK cleaning brand with strong vegan/cruelty-free positioning and thinner environmental disclosure.

environment.note: Cruelty Free International describes Astonish as a UK-made household brand with ethical positioning; broader environmental reporting is limited.

transparency.note: Public sustainability/ingredient disclosure is thinner than higher-scoring brands despite cruelty-free/vegan credentials.

packaging.note: Conventional recyclable plastic packaging keeps packaging score modest.

cruelty_free.note: Cruelty Free International lists Astonish as cruelty-free and vegan-approved.

accessibility.note: UK-manufactured budget brand with strong affordability and retail access.

products.name: ECOS cleaning products

environment.note: ECOS says more than 120 cleaning products are EPA Safer Choice-certified and the brand has won Safer Choice Partner of the Year repeatedly.

transparency.note: EPA Safer Choice listings and ECOS product pages provide ingredient and safer-chemistry accountability.

packaging.note: ECOS improves mainstream cleaner chemistry, but most formats still use conventional bottles rather than tablets or bulk refills.

cruelty_free.note: Leaping Bunny lists ECOS as certified cruelty-free.

accessibility.note: ECOS is sold through major US retailers and online, making it one of the most accessible safer-cleaning choices.

products.description: A broadly available safer-cleaning brand with EPA Safer Choice and Leaping Bunny signals, but conventional bottle formats.

products.name: Simple Green All-Purpose Cleaner
products.description: A familiar concentrated degreaser with EPA Safer Choice certification and strong access, but conventional plastic packaging and unclear cruelty-free certification.

environment.note: Simple Green says its All-Purpose Cleaner is EPA Safer Choice Certified and can be diluted up to 30x, reducing product volume per use.

transparency.note: Simple Green publishes SB-258 compliant ingredient disclosure pages for its household products.

packaging.note: Packaging FAQ says Simple Green uses PETE and HDPE plastic packaging and does not describe a plastic-free refill system.

cruelty_free.note: EWG notes leading certifiers PETA and Leaping Bunny have no information concerning Simple Green's animal-testing status.

accessibility.note: Sold broadly as a household, automotive and professional cleaner, with concentrate formats available through mainstream retail.

products.name: Puracy

environment.note: Puracy positions its formulas around USDA Certified Biobased ingredients and plant-derived cleaning chemistry.

transparency.note: EWG lists Puracy cleaner ratings and product ingredient disclosures for several cleaning products.

packaging.note: Puracy offers refills for some products, but most cleaning formats still depend on plastic bottles or pouches.

cruelty_free.note: Puracy says its products are PETA cruelty-free and not tested on animals.

accessibility.note: Puracy is easy to buy online and in some retail channels, but costs more than mainstream cleaners.

products.description: A popular biobased cleaner brand with visible EWG ingredient pages and cruelty-free claims, but mixed packaging.

products.name: Better Life

environment.note: EWG ingredient pages show plant-derived surfactants for Better Life all-purpose cleaners.

transparency.note: EWG lists Better Life products and ingredient disclosures across cleaning categories.

packaging.note: Better Life improves formula choices but is still mostly sold in conventional spray/plastic formats.

cruelty_free.note: Independent cruelty-free summaries report Better Life has confirmed no animal testing by brand, suppliers or third parties.

accessibility.note: Better Life is sold online and through major retail/marketplace channels at mid-market prices.

products.description: A plant-derived cleaner line with accessible prices and good EWG visibility, though packaging is conventional.

products.name: Bon Ami

environment.note: Bon Ami Powder Cleanser uses a simple abrasive powder format rather than a water-heavy spray cleaner.

transparency.note: Bon Ami FAQ explains current products and animal-derived ingredient status, but detailed ingredient disclosure is less modern than EWG leaders.

packaging.note: Powder format and canister packaging reduce water shipping, but it is not a full refill/tablet system.

cruelty_free.note: PETA lists Bon Ami / Faultless Starch as cruelty-free.

accessibility.note: Bon Ami is inexpensive and widely available in supermarkets, drugstores and online.

products.description: An old-school powder cleanser that is cheap, simple and cruelty-free, though less modern on certification and packaging.

products.name: Dawn dish soap
products.description: A dominant dish-soap default: excellent access and grease performance, with some PCR/refill packaging work but conventional formula and cruelty-free caveats.

environment.note: Dawn publishes product sustainability efforts, but the core line remains conventional dish liquid rather than a Safer Choice or refill-tablet model.

transparency.note: P&G SmartLabel publishes ingredients for Dawn Ultra Original, including surfactants and fragrance components.

packaging.note: Dawn says clear dishwashing-liquid bottles use 35% PCR plastic and Powerwash lets shoppers reuse the sprayer with refills.

cruelty_free.note: Dawn says P&G stopped testing consumer products on animals except where required by law, so it is not treated as fully cruelty-free certified.

accessibility.note: Dawn is one of the easiest dish soaps to find in US grocery, pharmacy, warehouse and online retail.

products.name: The Pink Stuff

environment.note: The Pink Stuff paste has a simple abrasive-cleaner profile, but EWG rates its multi-purpose cleaner C and flags ingredient concerns.

transparency.note: The brand publishes ingredient information, while EWG still rates disclosure and some ingredient concerns below leaders.

packaging.note: The Pink Stuff is sold in tubs and spray bottles, with no refill/plastic-free packaging model.

cruelty_free.note: The Pink Stuff says all products are approved by Cruelty Free International's Leaping Bunny programme.

accessibility.note: Very easy to find in mainstream US/UK retail and online at low prices.

products.description: A viral, affordable cleaning paste/spray line with strong cruelty-free certification but weaker ingredient and packaging scores.

products.name: Windex Original
products.description: A household glass-cleaner default with unusually visible ingredient disclosure, but ammonia/solvent concerns and no cruelty-free certification.

environment.note: EWG rates Windex Original D and flags fragrance, hexoxyethanol and ammonium hydroxide concerns, so it is not a low-impact formula leader.

transparency.note: SC Johnson's ingredient site publishes Windex Original ingredients and functions, including ammonia, solvents and surfactants.

packaging.note: SC Johnson says North American Windex PET bottles are now made with 100% recovered coastal plastic and that concentrated refills remain part of the line.

cruelty_free.note: SC Johnson says it uses non-animal methods where possible but complies with legal requirements for testing in countries that require it.

accessibility.note: Windex is a very widely available mainstream glass and surface cleaner in grocery, big-box and online retail.

products.name: Pine-Sol
products.description: A common multi-surface cleaner/disinfectant with clear ingredients and strong access, but conventional fragrance, plastic packaging and animal-testing caveats.

environment.note: Pine-Sol FAQ describes an EPA-registered disinfectant with fragrance and conventional surfactants, not a safer-choice or low-waste cleaner.

transparency.note: Pine-Sol FAQ publishes the Original Multi-Surface Cleaner ingredient list and use/dilution instructions.

packaging.note: FAQ says Pine-Sol bottles are #1 recyclable PET, but the product remains conventional bottled liquid rather than a refill/tablet system.

cruelty_free.note: PETA lists Pine-Sol (Clorox) as not cruelty-free.

accessibility.note: Pine-Sol is broadly available in mainstream US retail and online channels.

products.name: Lysol

environment.note: Lysol is designed around disinfecting claims and conventional chemical/aerosol/plastic formats rather than low-impact cleaning.

transparency.note: Reckitt publishes ingredient and safety data through its product-information site and SmartLabel-style pages.

packaging.note: Mainstream Lysol formats use conventional spray, wipe, aerosol and plastic packaging rather than refill/tablet systems.

cruelty_free.note: PETA lists Lysol / Reckitt Benckiser as not cruelty-free.

accessibility.note: Lysol is extremely widely available in grocery, pharmacy, big-box and online channels.

products.description: A disinfecting mainstream floor: unmatched availability and clear germ-kill use cases, but weak on low-impact, packaging and cruelty-free values.

products.name: Clorox
products.description: A conventional disinfectant and bleach-heavy household brand with broad access but weak low-impact and cruelty-free alignment.

environment.note: Clorox has some EcoClean/Safer Choice initiatives but mainstream disinfectants and plastic packaging keep impact score low.

transparency.note: Clorox says it shares U.S. cleaning, disinfecting and laundry ingredients through SmartLabel, including safety and environmental information.

packaging.note: Clorox reports packaging sustainability initiatives, but conventional plastic remains common.

cruelty_free.note: Clorox policy allows animal testing where legally required and does not carry a Leaping Bunny-style certification.

accessibility.note: Very broad US retail availability and low mainstream prices.

products.name: Tide (P&G)
products.description: A dominant mainstream laundry brand with some packaging experiments, but mostly conventional high-volume detergent formats.

environment.note: P&G/Tide report sustainability efforts such as Tide EVO and packaging goals, but mainstream liquid/pod detergent remains high-volume conventional product.

transparency.note: Tide/P&G publish materials and sustainability pages, but formula and impact transparency remain partial.

packaging.note: P&G highlights Tide EVO no-plastic-bottle packaging, while conventional bottles and pods remain widely sold.

cruelty_free.note: PETA lists Tide/Procter & Gamble as not cruelty-free.

accessibility.note: Tide is globally available and cheap/easy to find, with many mainstream formats.

products.name: Force of Nature
products.description: An electrolyzed-water system that makes cleaner/disinfectant at home from capsules, with strong certification signals but higher upfront cost.

environment.note: Force of Nature lists EPA registration plus Green Seal and carbon-neutral certifications, and its system avoids shipping ready-to-use plastic bottles.

transparency.note: Certification page and EPA label disclose the on-demand disinfectant model and approved-use constraints.

packaging.note: Reusable appliance/bottle plus small activator capsules greatly reduce single-use cleaner bottles, though capsules and device hardware remain.

cruelty_free.note: Leaping Bunny highlights Force of Nature as certified cruelty-free.

accessibility.note: Mostly direct-to-consumer with a starter-device cost, so it is less accessible than grocery-store sprays.

products.name: Aunt Fannie's
products.description: A vinegar-centered cleaner line with strong EWG and cruelty-free signals, but mostly conventional bottle and wipe formats.

environment.note: EWG lists Aunt Fannie's all-purpose and floor-cleaning products with A ratings across many vinegar-based cleaners.

transparency.note: EWG product pages disclose ingredient lists for Aunt Fannie's floor and vinegar cleaners.

packaging.note: Formula quality is strong, but packaging is still mostly bottles and wipes rather than a tablet/refill system.

cruelty_free.note: EWG indicates Aunt Fannie's products carry the Leaping Bunny cruelty-free mark.

accessibility.note: Available online and in some retail channels, but less ubiquitous than mainstream cleaners.

products.name: Frosch
products.description: A European eco-cleaning brand with recycled-plastic bottles, vegan formulas, and a long record in lower-impact household cleaners.

environment.note: Frosch says its cleaners use natural-based active ingredients, are microplastic-free, and come from an eco-cleaning brand dating to 1986.

transparency.note: Frosch publishes sustainability and FAQ pages explaining its eco-quality, formulas, and packaging approach.

packaging.note: Frosch says its PET and PE cleaning-product bottles are made of 100% recycled plastic and designed for closed-loop recycling.

cruelty_free.note: Frosch FAQ says formulas are vegan; public certification evidence is weaker than Leaping Bunny/PETA-listed brands, so cruelty-free score is moderate.

accessibility.note: Widely available in parts of Europe, but less accessible for U.S. shoppers.

products.name: Biokleen cleaning products
products.description: A plant- and mineral-based cleaning brand with cruelty-free evidence, though current product availability and packaging are less compelling than top refill systems.

environment.note: Biokleen says its green cleaners are plant/mineral based, contain no VOCs, and avoid several conventional harsh ingredients.

transparency.note: Biokleen provides brand-level ingredient and safety claims, but fewer product-level modern disclosures than EWG-heavy leaders.

packaging.note: Cleaning formulas are lower-impact, but the brand is not primarily a plastic-free tablet or refill-system option.

cruelty_free.note: PETA lists Biokleen as cruelty-free and says ingredients, finished products, suppliers, and third parties follow that standard.

accessibility.note: PETA lists Biokleen availability through drugstores, health food stores, internet, mail order, and supermarkets, but it is not as ubiquitous as mainstream cleaners.

products.name: Bar Keepers Friend
products.description: A cheap, long-running powder cleanser that avoids bleach and water-heavy spray format, but is not a green-certified low-tox leader.

environment.note: Brand explains most formulas rely on oxalic acid rather than bleach, but EWG notes the cookware cleanser is not certified as a green cleaner and carries handling warnings.

transparency.note: FAQ and product information explain active ingredients and product-use constraints, but ingredient transparency is less complete than SmartLabel/EWG leaders.

packaging.note: Powder format avoids shipping mostly water and the can is recyclable, though it is not a reusable refill system.

cruelty_free.note: Bar Keepers Friend FAQ says the brand does not test on animals.

accessibility.note: Widely sold, inexpensive, and common in grocery, hardware, big-box, and online channels.

products.name: Mr. Clean
products.description: A widely available mainstream P&G cleaning brand with strong access and ingredient disclosure, but weak low-impact and cruelty-free signals.

environment.note: SmartLabel ingredient pages show conventional formulas rather than a Safer Choice, refill, or low-impact cleaner standard.

transparency.note: P&G provides SmartLabel ingredient disclosure for Mr. Clean all-purpose and spray products.

packaging.note: Mr. Clean is primarily sold in conventional plastic bottles, sprays, and single-use cleaning formats rather than low-waste refills.

cruelty_free.note: PETA lists Mr. Clean / Procter & Gamble as not cruelty-free.

accessibility.note: Extremely accessible mainstream cleaner sold through grocery, pharmacy, big-box, and online channels.

products.name: Boulder Clean
products.description: A US cleaning brand with EPA Safer Choice products, Leaping Bunny certification and better-than-mainstream ingredient signals.

environment.note: Boulder Clean says it offers a wide variety of EPA Safer Choice-certified dish, surface, laundry and disinfectant cleaners.

transparency.note: The brand explains its Safer Choice and Leaping Bunny certifications on a public labels/certifications page.

packaging.note: Boulder Clean uses conventional liquid-cleaner packaging rather than a tablet/refill model, so packaging score stays moderate.

cruelty_free.note: Boulder Clean states that it is Leaping Bunny Certified.

accessibility.note: Sold online and through US retail channels, but with less reach than major mass-market cleaners.

products.name: Lemi Shine
products.description: A citric-acid-based cleaning line with strong EPA Safer Choice evidence and good mainstream availability.

environment.note: Lemi Shine says many products are EPA Safer Choice certified and use safer ingredients such as citric extracts.

transparency.note: Lemi Shine publicly announced Safer Choice certification and discusses the certification basis on its site.

packaging.note: Product formats are mostly conventional powders, liquids and dishwasher/dish-care packs rather than a reusable-refill system.

cruelty_free.note: No Leaping Bunny/PETA-style cruelty-free certification was found on the cited brand certification pages.

accessibility.note: Lemi Shine is sold through major US retailers and online channels, with mainstream dish and cleaning products.

products.name: JAWS Cleaners
products.description: A just-add-water refill-pod cleaning system with several EPA Safer Choice formulas and much stronger packaging logic than conventional sprays.

environment.note: JAWS says several cleaners are EPA Safer Choice products and that its refillable system is designed to reduce plastic waste.

transparency.note: JAWS provides a Safer Choice product page with EPA disclaimer language and ingredient-disclosure context.

packaging.note: JAWS says its reusable bottle plus refill pod system saves 83% of plastic waste compared with traditional spray cleaners.

cruelty_free.note: The reviewed JAWS product and Safer Choice pages did not present an independent cruelty-free certification.

accessibility.note: JAWS is available online and through select retailers, but is less common than conventional spray-cleaner brands.

products.name: CleanWell
products.description: A thymol-based disinfectant line that can meet a real disinfection need without defaulting to bleach or quats.

environment.note: CleanWell says its plant-derived thymol disinfectants are EPA-registered and avoid bleach, ammonia and alcohol formulas.

transparency.note: CleanWell FAQ explains thymol, EPA toxicity category context and use around households.

packaging.note: CleanWell relies mostly on conventional spray/wipe formats rather than a concentrated refill system.

cruelty_free.note: Cruelty-Free Kitty lists CleanWell as cruelty-free after checking finished products, ingredients, suppliers and third parties.

accessibility.note: Available online and in some retail channels, but less common than Lysol, Clorox or Scrubbing Bubbles.

products.name: The Unscented Company
products.description: A Canadian fragrance-free household brand with B Corp status, Leaping Bunny certification and strong refill packaging signals.

environment.note: The Unscented Company frames its products around reducing collective impact and unscented home/body care.

transparency.note: Its company history page documents B Corp certification and Leaping Bunny certification milestones.

packaging.note: The brand prominently sells refill boxes and reusable/refillable product formats.

cruelty_free.note: The company says it chose Leaping Bunny certification as its seal of approval for its no-animal-testing commitment.

accessibility.note: Online US/Canada access is good, but brick-and-mortar reach is narrower than mainstream household brands.

products.name: Koala Eco
products.description: A plant-based, botanical cleaning brand with Leaping Bunny certification and premium niche availability.

environment.note: Koala Eco is described by Oceanic Society as creating plant-based products using natural, sustainable ingredients.

transparency.note: Koala Eco publishes certification and cruelty-free information, but with less third-party ingredient-screening evidence than EWG/Safer Choice leaders.

packaging.note: The line is mostly premium bottled liquid cleaners rather than a broad tablet/refill-pod system.

cruelty_free.note: Leaping Bunny lists Koala Eco as certified and describes the range as vegan and cruelty-free.

accessibility.note: Premium pricing and niche distribution make Koala Eco less accessible than grocery-store cleaners.

products.name: Eco-Me
products.description: A smaller plant-based cleaner brand with Leaping Bunny/PETA signals and a natural-products orientation.

environment.note: Eco-Me says its products follow Natural Products Association guidelines and have top ratings from Green Seal/EWG-style sources.

transparency.note: Eco-Me publishes an accomplishments page listing certification and rating claims, though not the same depth as Safer Choice product lists.

packaging.note: The product line uses conventional bottles rather than a strong refill/tablet packaging model.

cruelty_free.note: Eco-Me says it is PETA and Leaping Bunny certified and uses no animal testing or by-products.

accessibility.note: Eco-Me has online access but narrower mainstream retail reach than larger brands.

products.name: 9 Elements
products.description: A P&G vinegar-powered line with EWG/Safer Choice signals, but still under a large conventional parent and mostly conventional packaging.

environment.note: 9 Elements describes plant-based, vinegar-powered cleaning solutions with no more than 9 ingredients.

transparency.note: EWG lists 9 Elements Bathroom Cleaner as a certified green cleaner and EWG Verified product.

packaging.note: 9 Elements earns ingredient-certification credit, but remains mostly liquid cleaners/detergents in plastic bottles.

cruelty_free.note: P&G says it no longer animal-tests consumer products unless required by law; 9 Elements itself was not found as a Leaping Bunny-certified brand.

accessibility.note: As a P&G line, 9 Elements has stronger mainstream retail access than most niche greener brands.

products.name: CLR
products.description: A widely sold calcium/lime/rust specialty cleaner with unusually strong EPA Safer Choice partner evidence for a mainstream-ish chemical cleaner.

environment.note: CLR Brands says its CLR products meet EPA Safer Choice health and environmental standards.

transparency.note: CLR's Safer Choice page explains the EPA certification disclaimer and the brand's decade of Safer Choice recognition.

packaging.note: CLR is mostly sold in conventional plastic bottles rather than refill concentrates or tablets.

cruelty_free.note: CLR's reviewed Safer Choice and brand pages did not present an independent cruelty-free certification.

accessibility.note: CLR is broadly sold through mainstream home-improvement, grocery and big-box channels at accessible prices.

products.name: OxiClean
products.description: A very accessible oxygen-cleaner and stain-remover brand with ingredient disclosure, but weak cruelty-free and low-waste credentials.

environment.note: Church & Dwight ingredient disclosure for OxiClean powder lists sodium carbonate and sodium carbonate peroxide, but the line is not framed as a green-certified cleaner.

transparency.note: Church & Dwight publishes ingredient-disclosure forms for OxiClean products.

packaging.note: Powder formats avoid shipping only liquid, but tubs/sprays remain conventional packaging rather than refill systems.

cruelty_free.note: PETA lists OxiClean / Church & Dwight as not cruelty-free.

accessibility.note: OxiClean is a mass-market stain-remover brand available widely across retail channels.

products.name: Scrubbing Bubbles

products.name: All-in-One Dishwasher Tablets
products.description: A widely recognized eco-dishwasher tablet line, stronger on plant-based ingredients and cardboard packaging than mainstream pods, but still a purchased single-use tablet.

environment.note: Ecover says its all-in-one dishwasher tablets use biodegradable ingredients and are designed to run on eco mode.

transparency.note: The product page states tablet role, scent variants, pack sizes, rinse-aid/salt action, and ingredient positioning.

packaging.note: Ecover's cited product page says the box is made with 100% recycled cardboard.

cruelty_free.note: Ecover says it has been Leaping Bunny certified since 2011 and follows Cruelty Free International standards.

accessibility.note: Available through UK/EU Ecover channels and retailers, but less universal globally than Finish or Cascade.

products.name: Pure Power Dishwasher Detergent Packs
products.description: A biobased dishwasher-pack option from a B Corp cleaning marketplace, useful for shoppers already using Grove's refill and lower-plastic ecosystem.

environment.note: Grove's product page presents Pure Power Dishwasher Detergent Packs as a dishwasher pack made with bio-based ingredients.

transparency.note: The product listing shows format, scent/free-clear positioning, load count, and ingredient/safety framing.

packaging.note: Grove product imagery/text describes compostable packaging, but the cleaner is still a dishwasher-pack format rather than a loose tablet.

cruelty_free.note: Grove's marketplace and brand positioning emphasize vetted home products and lower-impact standards, but the cited page is less explicit than Leaping Bunny pages.

accessibility.note: Mostly direct/online marketplace access, convenient for subscribers but less ubiquitous than supermarket dishwasher packs.

products.name: Platinum Plus ActionPacs
products.description: The highly recognizable US dishwasher-pod floor: strong convenience and performance claims with ingredient disclosure, but weak packaging and values signals.

environment.note: Cascade positions Platinum Plus for strong cleaning performance, but the product remains a conventional single-dose pod from a mainstream chemical brand.

transparency.note: P&G SmartLabel lists ingredients for Cascade Platinum Plus ActionPacs, giving stronger disclosure than an unlabeled floor option.

packaging.note: The product is sold as conventional ActionPacs rather than a loose, refill, or plastic-free tablet system.

cruelty_free.note: No third-party cruelty-free certification is presented on the cited product or SmartLabel pages.

accessibility.note: Cascade is a mass-market US dishwasher brand with broad retail availability and prominent product-line pages.

products.name: Quantum Dishwasher Tablets
products.description: A globally recognizable dishwasher-tablet floor with good ingredient disclosure and no-pre-rinse messaging, but conventional pod/tablet tradeoffs.

environment.note: Finish says Quantum is designed for no pre-rinsing, which can reduce wasted water, but the product remains a conventional mainstream dishwasher tablet.

transparency.note: RBNAinfo publishes ingredient information for Finish Quantum tabs, including surfactants and sodium percarbonate.

packaging.note: The cited line is a conventional dishwasher-tablet/pod format rather than a refill or plastic-free loose-tablet system.

cruelty_free.note: No third-party cruelty-free certification is presented on the cited Finish product or ingredient pages.

accessibility.note: Finish Quantum is a mainstream dishwasher-tablet line with broad retail recognition and regional product pages.
